findings.claim: Nine places name the exam board to students (“For the Eduqas GCSE”, “the Eduqas specification”, “Eduqas GCSE Music Component 3”), two of them with the component code.
findings.truth: House rule: this board is never named in student-facing text, and component codes are not used.

findings.claim: “I Wanna Hold Your Hand” by The Beatles uses 32-bar song form.
findings.truth: The title is “I Want to Hold Your Hand” (1963) and the form is a modified 32-bar form.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: I Want to Hold Your Hand

findings.claim: Q3 is labelled 4 marks; its scheme says “Award up to 3 marks” and then lists four 1-mark points.
findings.truth: The four points are worth 4 marks, matching the label.

findings.claim: Five questions labelled “1 mark” or “4 marks” whose own mark schemes award 2 or 3.
findings.truth: The label is the number the AI marker marks out of (js/main.js reads the first number in type), so it must match the scheme.

findings.claim: Six questions labelled 10 marks whose band ladders stop at 6 or 8, so the top of the label is unreachable.
findings.truth: Relabel each to the total its own ladder covers.

findings.claim: conjunct = “Movement by step (conjunct) or by leap (disjunct) in a melody.”
findings.truth: Conjunct is movement by step only; disjunct is movement by leap. The entry defines both at once, so it can be read either way.
findings.evidence: standard musical definition; spec glossary lists conjunct and disjunct separately

findings.claim: Two discussion questions labelled “12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)”.
findings.truth: Neither uses a printed extract, a score or sub-questions, and both ladders stop at 8: they are 8-mark extended responses.
findings.evidence: spec Component 3 assessment section; the questions themselves

findings.claim: Two cloze cards (“_____ became hugely popular in the 1980s…”) with one-word answers.
findings.truth: House format: a one-word answer needs a question opening with What/Which/Who/When/Name.

findings.claim: The tabla is taught as a traditional bhangra instrument in both lessons and is credited in four mark schemes.
findings.truth: The spec's own AoS4 list says “dhol drum (not the tabla)”. The tabla belongs to Indian classical music; a student naming it for bhangra follows the lesson into a wrong answer.
findings.evidence: spec AoS4 glossary, Bhangra bullet list

findings.claim: “pentatonic melodies, and marimbas … as heard in Toto's Africa”
findings.truth: The marimba/kalimba riff in Africa is synthesised: Steve Porcaro programmed it on a Yamaha GS-1 and it was layered six times. No acoustic marimba plays it.

findings.claim: MADTSHRIT expanded here as …Tempo…Texture; lesson 5 and the film music unit expand it as …Texture…Tonality.
findings.truth: One expansion only. The house version (lesson 5, film music L5) ends with Tonality.

findings.claim: A Key Fact reproduces a past-paper question and its accepted answers: “In a typical exam question, a bhangra question asked students to identify the tempo (allegro), the tonality (…) … Accepted answers included: …”
findings.truth: House rule bars board questions, mark-scheme wording and indicative content. The listening advice is kept, the paper and its answer list are not.

findings.claim: Q6 ends “Quality of written communication will be assessed.”
findings.truth: The appraising paper assesses AO3 and AO4 only (20% + 20%); the spec sets no written-communication or SPaG marks anywhere.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 assessment objectives and weightings; no SPaG section in the spec

findings.claim: “The intro uses a riff pattern with chords I–vii–iii (A–G#m–C#m).”
findings.truth: The chord letters are right but the numerals are not: in A major the 7th degree carries G sharp diminished, so G#m cannot be vii. The intro centres on C sharp minor (VI–v–i).
findings.evidence: Hooktheory analysis of Africa (intro: C# minor, VI v i7); basic diatonic harmony

findings.claim: “chord vi (F#m) and chord IV (D) include one primary and one secondary chord”
findings.truth: The same paragraph has already said primary chords are I, IV and V, and the practice key says D (IV) is primary and F#m (vi) secondary. Say it plainly.
findings.evidence: internal consistency with practice Q3 key

findings.claim: “In the exam you will hear each extract twice (sometimes three times for longer questions).”
findings.truth: The spec sets no number of playings; the number is printed on the paper for each extract.
findings.evidence: spec Component 3 assessment section (silent on playings)

findings.claim: phasing = “two slightly detuned copies of a signal”
findings.truth: Phasing offsets the copies in time, not in tuning — which is what lesson 3 teaches and what its mark scheme credits. Detuning is a different effect.
findings.evidence: lesson 3 content and mark scheme; standard definition

findings.claim: Q2 asks for two features; the scheme awards one mark per feature up to 4 marks under a 4-mark label.
findings.truth: Ask for four features so the question, the scheme and the label agree.

findings.claim: “Give one clear answer — do not write two options, as only the first will be marked.”
findings.truth: Plausible exam-technique advice but not stated anywhere in the spec. Left alone.

findings.claim: The unit never tells students that Africa (Toto, 1982) is the prepared extract they must study in depth for this area of study.
findings.truth: It is covered by the separate toto-africa unit, so no edit here; worth knowing the popular-music unit does not signpost it.

summary: Every lesson needed work. The serious items are the tabla taught and credited as a bhangra instrument against the spec's explicit “not the tabla”, a Key Fact that reproduces a past-paper question with its accepted answers, a false written-communication claim, and a chord analysis in the Africa worked example that labels G#m as vii of A major. The rest are board naming, mark labels that disagree with their own schemes, and definition drift between lessons.
